summary:
Mars Walk Guardian is an interactive Mars surface-routing prototype created for the “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge.

The project converts a NASA HiRISE stereo elevation model near Curiosity’s Sol 4621 location in Gale Crater into a 201 × 201 terrain-planning grid. A Python weighted A* planner rejects infeasible movements and evaluates the remaining routes using distance, modeled terrain risk, energy consumption, and a required battery reserve.

The application presents the calculated path through synchronized 2D tactical and 3D rover views. During the demonstration, a simulated obstruction blocks part of the original return corridor. The planner calculates a different feasible route around it and estimates the battery remaining at the simulated Gale Base.

Measured NASA data, derived terrain properties, and simulated operational inputs are labeled separately. The current prototype uses a simulated rover as a terrain scout and crew-support asset. Future development would extend the system with astronaut-specific Marswalk constraints such as oxygen, walk-back distance, thermal exposure, and radiation.
details:
THE PROBLEM

Future explorers on Mars will need to make surface-navigation decisions without immediate help from Earth. A planned corridor may become unavailable because of terrain, an obstruction, equipment constraints, or limited energy. A useful Martian map should therefore do more than show a location. It should help an explorer evaluate whether a route remains feasible and explain why another route was selected.

OUR SOLUTION

Mars Walk Guardian demonstrates the terrain-routing and emergency-replanning layer of a future Martian surface-planning system. The current prototype uses a simulated rover as a terrain scout and crew-support asset near Mount Sharp in Gale Crater.

The user can inspect a calculated route in a 2D tactical map and replay the same backend-generated path in a 3D rover view. When a simulated obstruction appears in the return corridor, the application requests a new route and displays the detour, its distance, modeled terrain risk, energy use, and estimated battery remaining.

HOW THE ROUTING WORKS

A Python FastAPI backend loads and caches a 201 × 201 HiRISE-derived terrain grid containing 40,401 valid cells. The grid uses approximately 1.012 metres between elevation samples.

The weighted A* planner first rejects infeasible movements, including:

• Invalid or blocked terrain cells

• Movements exceeding the project’s along-route slope threshold

• Cells exceeding the conservative local-slope proxy threshold

• Simulated slip-risk values at or above the configured limit

• Routes that would violate the modeled battery reserve

The planner then evaluates feasible movements using distance, modeled terrain risk, and normalized energy use. The demonstration uses a 10 Wh minimum battery reserve and a project assumption of 0.25 Wh per metre.

DEMONSTRATION RESULT

The recorded outbound route is 85.74 m. After the application introduces a simulated obstruction, the planner calculates a 90.48 m emergency return route that travels around the blocked area.

The detour adds 4.74 m. Beginning with a simulated emergency battery state of 65 Wh, the application estimates that the rover reaches the simulated Gale Base with 42.38 Wh remaining, maintaining the required 10 Wh reserve.

In a supplied benchmark of 12 local runs on this terrain grid, both recorded routes came within one percent of the shortest feasible traversable distance. Median local calculation time remained below 0.3 seconds for both recorded scenarios. These measurements describe this demonstration configuration and are not general flight-performance claims.

DATA PROVENANCE

Measured:

• Elevation from a NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE stereo terrain model

Derived:

• Grid coordinates

• Terrain aspect

• Local roughness

• A conservative local-slope magnitude proxy

Simulated:

• Gale Base

• Obstruction placement

• Wheel-slip risk

• Rover battery state

• Energy-consumption parameters

The interface and documentation label these categories separately so that simulated telemetry is not represented as measured NASA evidence.

TECHNOLOGY

• React and TypeScript frontend

• MapLibre GL JS tactical map

• Interactive 3D rover visualization

• Python FastAPI routing backend

• Weighted A* path planning

• Server-side cached HiRISE terrain grid

• Automated Python routing and terrain tests

RELATION TO THE CHALLENGE

The “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge asks teams to create an integrated view of a Martian location or route using NASA mission data to support safe exploration and science.

Mars Walk Guardian contributes an explainable routing and emergency-replanning component. NASA terrain data directly determines which movements the planner considers feasible and how the candidate routes are evaluated.

The current prototype models a rover rather than a complete astronaut Marswalk. It can represent an autonomous precursor, terrain scout, or crew-support rover. Future development would add astronaut-specific constraints, including oxygen, radiation exposure, thermal limits, communications, travel time, and maximum walk-back distance.

LIMITATIONS

This project is an educational simulation and is not flight-certified or suitable for operational navigation. The local-slope value is a conservative magnitude proxy rather than direction-specific cross-slope. Wheel-slip risk and obstruction placement are simulated. The one-metre terrain grid cannot resolve every wheel-scale rock or surface hazard. The science candidate is linked to a Curiosity waypoint, but its exact geology has not been confirmed.
